title: AI Has a God Problem Stretching From the Vatican to the Baptist Pulpit
source_used: Mint (carries the Wall Street Journal text by Tim Higgins; WSJ page itself returned 401)
key_facts: Religious leaders are weighing AI's potential benefits against fears that it could threaten human dignity, jobs and community well-being, creating a new political risk for AI makers (WSJ, Tim Higgins).
Pope Leo XIV published an encyclical in May on 'safeguarding the human person in the time of artificial intelligence' and compared AI to the Tower of Babel.
The National Association of Evangelicals issued an AI policy statement earlier this month; the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) held an AI summit in August.

Pastor Joseph Hutchinson of Gospel Light Baptist Church, Orangeburg, South Carolina, told the WSJ the anxiety he hears about AI outranks wars and the economy, and warned in a sermon that 'AI wants to be God'.
The risk for companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic is getting further at odds with a large part of the US public, some already unhappy with data centers and Flock cameras.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman distanced his company from a New York Times report that Anthropic unsuccessfully lobbied the Vatican to change its view on whether AI could be conscious, saying he is uncomfortable with people ascribing religious force to AI models.
Walter Kim, president of the National Association of Evangelicals, said the faith community is having a moment because AI raises the question of what it means to be human.
quote_evidence: Already a polarizing political issue this fall, the AI industry's latest challenge is emerging from the pulpit.
The risk for the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic is getting further sideways with a large swath of the American populace
Those raising concerns can't be dismissed as simply Luddites.
why_it_matters_hint: Churches and religious leaders are becoming a channel for public worry about AI, a new political pressure on AI companies.
notes: WSJ page returned 401. Read the WSJ text (Tim Higgins) on Mint, which carries it verbatim under the WSJ byline; credit stays with the Wall Street Journal. A feature of interviews and statements, not polling.
